solve-q-r26-t03-03.d: 0 < x < 1 → order of x², x, √x, 1/x (plug in x = ¼; or know the range table)

solve-q-r26-t04-02.d: 51² − 49² = ? (difference of squares: 2·100 = 200; or the long way; trap: (51−49)² = 4)

solve-q-r26-t04-03.d: which equals (a−b)² for all a, b ((b−a)² = (a−b)², the square kills the minus; or plug in 5, 2)

solve-q-r26-t04-04.t: Given: x+\frac{1}{x}=3 (x\ne0). What is the value of x^2+\frac{1}{x^2}?
solve-q-r26-t04-04.d: x + 1/x = 3, find x² + 1/x² (square both sides, middle term is 2 → 7; trap 9)

solve-q-r26-t05-02.d: 98·102 − 99·101 = ? (sum times difference around 100; 100² cancels → −4 + 1 = −3; trap: lost minus gives −5)

solve-q-r26-t05-03.d: given a−b=3, (b−a)²+2a−2b = ? (use the block: 9+6 = 15; or plug in a=3, b=0)

solve-q-r26-t05-04.d: (a²b+ab²)/ab = ? (ones give a three-way tie → new numbers a=2, b=3; or take out ab → a+b)

solve-q-r26-t05-17.d: (x³ + x²y)/(x + y) − xy = ? (count the powers: power 2 → only x(x − y); then factor and cancel to confirm)

solve-q-r26-t05-18.d: ((a + b)² − (a − b)²)/2a = ? (plug in ones → three-way tie, broken by counting powers → 2b; then the algebra: 4ab/2a)

solve-q-r26-t06-01.d: (x+2)/3 − (x−4)/6 = x/2 (multiply by 6, minus hits the whole numerator → x=4; or test the choices; trap gives 0)

solve-q-r26-t06-02.d: (2x + 1)/(x − 2) = (x + 3)/(x − 2) (restriction first: algebra gives forbidden x = 2 → no solution; or test the choices)

solve-q-r26-t06-03.d: 5x+3y=41, 3x+5y=39, find x+y (add the equations: 8(x+y) = 80 → 10; the long way shown for contrast)

solve-q-r26-t06-04.t: Given: x > 0 and y > 0, and \begin{cases} xy=20 \\ \frac{x}{y}=5 \end{cases} x-y = ?
solve-q-r26-t06-04.d: x, y > 0, xy = 20, x/y = 5, find x − y (multiply the equations: x² = 100 → 8; or substitution x = 5y)

solve-q-r26-t07-01.d: x²y = 18, xy² = 12, find x/y (divide the equations → 18/12 = 3/2; check with x = 3, y = 2; trap: upside-down 2/3)

solve-q-r26-t07-02.d: x+1/x = 6, find x²+1/x² (square both sides, middle term is 2 → 34; trap 36; with a minus it is −2)

solve-q-r26-t07-05.d: (x + 1)² = (x − 3)², find x (equal squares → equal or opposite: x = 1; or expand both; trap: 'no solution')

solve-q-r26-t08-01.d: 2ⁿ+2ⁿ+2ⁿ+2ⁿ = ? (count the copies: 4·2ⁿ = 2^(n+2); check n=1, tie → n=2; bases never add)

solve-q-r26-t08-02.d: 0 < x < 1, which is smallest: x, x², x³, x⁻²? (plug in 1/2 → x³; x⁻² flips to 4)

solve-q-r26-t08-05.d: x³y² < 0, what is necessarily true? (even power hides the sign, odd keeps it → x < 0)

solve-q-r26-t09-01.d: ⁴√(9⁶) = ? (power over index: 9^(6/4) = 9^(3/2) = 27; or write 9 = 3² → 3¹²; trap: subtracting 6 − 4)

solve-q-r26-t09-02.d: which is largest: 5.2, 3√3, 2√7, √26 (square each / bring numbers inside the root: 27.04, 27, 28, 26)

solve-q-r26-t09-03.d: √(x+6) = x, find x (plug in the choices; −2 is a fake solution from squaring, a root is never negative)

solve-q-r26-t09-04.d: 0 < x < 1, largest of x², x, √x, x³ (plug in x = 1/4; rule: between 0 and 1 powers shrink, the root grows)

solve-q-r26-t09-05.d: largest of √3, ⁶√28, ³√5, ⁶√26 (raise all to the 6th power to clear every root: 27, 28, 25, 26)

solve-q-r26-t09-06.d: 1/(√3 − √2) = ? (multiply by the partner √3 + √2, bottom becomes 1; or check: choice × bottom = 1)

solve-q-r26-t10-01.d: √(2x+3) = x, find x (x ≥ 0 rules out −1, then try choices; or square and check in the original — −1 is fake)

solve-q-r26-t10-02.d: 2¹⁰ + 2¹⁰ + 2¹⁰ + 2¹⁰ = ? (count the copies: 4 · 2¹⁰ = 2¹²; check with small numbers; traps 2⁴⁰, 8¹⁰)

solve-q-r26-t10-03.d: 3^(x+2) − 3ˣ = 72, find x (take out the smallest power: 8 · 3ˣ = 72; or try the choices from the middle)

solve-q-r26-t11-01.d: 1/(√5 − 2) − 1/(√5 + 2) = ? (conjugates: each bottom becomes 1 → 4; or estimate with √5 ≈ 2.24)

solve-q-r26-t11-02.d: x > 0, ³√(x√x) = 2, find x (write roots as powers: x^(1/2) = 2 → x = 4; or try the choices)

solve-q-r26-t12-03.t: Given: \begin{cases} a>b \\ c>d \end{cases} Which of the following is necessarily true?

solve-q-r26-t12-04.t: Given: \begin{cases} -2<x<5 \\ 1<y<4 \end{cases} What is the range of x-y?

solve-q-r26-t13-01.d: |2x − 1| = 7, all values of x (two cases: inside = 7 or −7 → x = 4 or −3; check both); restored from your Hebrew lesson (2026-10-08): the general rule for equations with bars — the left side equals the right side, or minus the right side (the same left side twice) — and the wording point: "all the values" needs both, "could be" needs only one (often only one is offered) · 2026-10-08 (later): the general rule is now in the lesson → reminder "As in the lesson: the same left side, twice"; the wording line shortened to "Here they ask for ALL the values — so we need both"

solve-q-r26-t13-02.t: Which of the following has no solution?
solve-q-r26-t13-02.d: which has no solution: |x+2| < −1 etc. (look at the right side: bars are never below a negative number)

solve-q-r26-t13-03.t: Given: |x+4|=3x. Which of the following gives all the possible values of x?
solve-q-r26-t13-03.d: |x + 4| = 3x, all values of x (two cases, then check: −1 is fake; or 3x ≥ 0 so x ≥ 0 → only 2)

solve-q-r26-t13-13.d: |a| = 7, |b| = 3, |a+b| < |a−b|, find |a+b| (smaller sum → opposite signs → 7 − 3 = 4; or try 4 sign cases)

solve-q-r26-t13-15.t: Given: a^2+b^2=2ab+9. Which of the following is necessarily true?
solve-q-r26-t13-15.d: a² + b² = 2ab + 9, necessarily true? (mirror test: swap and flip leave only |a − b| = 3; algebra: (a − b)² = 9)

solve-q-r26-t14-01.t: Which of the following numbers is prime?
solve-q-r26-t14-01.d: which is prime: 91, 119, 113, 133 (divide by primes up to √n; three fakes split by 7, so 113 is prime)

solve-q-r26-t14-03.t: a and b are positive integers. Given: 2^a\cdot3^b=108. a-b=?
solve-q-r26-t14-03.d: 2^a·3^b = 108, find a − b (break 108 into primes 2²·3³ and match exponents; trap swaps a and b)

solve-q-r26-t15-01.t: a and b are positive integers, and a>b. When a is divided by 7, the remainder is 2. When b is divided by 7, the remainder is 5. What will be the remainder if a-b is divided by 7?
solve-q-r26-t15-01.d: a leaves 2, b leaves 5 when divided by 7, find remainder of a − b (subtract remainders, add 7 if negative; check with numbers)

solve-q-r26-t15-15.t: x and y are positive integers. x is divisible by 6, and y is divisible by 9. What is the largest number that x+y is necessarily divisible by?
solve-q-r26-t15-15.d: x divisible by 6, y by 9, largest sure divisor of x + y (tag it: 6k + 9m = 3(2k + 3m); trap: equal values)

solve-q-r26-t16-01.t: Given: \begin{cases} x<0<y \\ x+y>0 \end{cases} Which of the following is necessarily true?
solve-q-r26-t16-01.d: x < 0 < y, x + y > 0, what is surely true (mixed signs: the bigger size wins → |y| > |x|; check with numbers)

solve-q-r26-t16-02.t: The sum of seven consecutive integers is 91. What is the largest of them?
solve-q-r26-t16-02.d: 7 consecutive integers sum to 91, find the largest (sum = count × middle → middle 13; or algebra 7b = 91)

solve-q-r26-t16-03.t: The sum of four consecutive integers is always —
solve-q-r26-t16-03.d: sum of 4 consecutive integers is always — (write 4a + 6: even, not divisible by 4; counterexample for 3)

solve-q-r26-t16-04.t: n is a positive odd number. The product n(n+2)(n+4) is necessarily divisible by —
solve-q-r26-t16-04.d: n odd, n(n+2)(n+4) surely divisible by (smallest case 15 is only a candidate; test 7·9·11 avoiding 5 → 3)

solve-q-r26-t17-01.t: The figure shows the numbers a, b, c and d on a number line (the figure is not drawn to scale). Which of the following is necessarily negative?
solve-q-r26-t17-01.d: letters on a number line, which is surely negative (write each letter's range; not to scale → trust order only)

solve-q-r26-t17-02.t: The figure shows the number x and the points K, L, M and N on a number line (the figure is not drawn to scale). Which of the points could represent the number \sqrt{x}?
solve-q-r26-t17-02.d: x between 0 and 1 on a line, where can √x be (root of a positive fraction is bigger, still below 1)

solve-q-r26-t17-03.t: Given: -4<x<-2. Which of the following is necessarily true?
solve-q-r26-t17-03.d: −4 < x < −2, range of 6/x (flip with reciprocal then ×6, or plug in the two ends)

solve-q-r26-t17-04.t: Given: x<-1<y<0. Which of the following is necessarily true?
solve-q-r26-t17-04.d: x < −1 < y < 0, which is surely true (test at the edges x = −2, y = −½)

solve-q-r26-t17-05.t: On a number line, point A is at -7 and point B is at 5. Point C is between A and B, and its distance from A is one third of the distance AB. What number is at point C?
solve-q-r26-t17-05.d: A = −7, B = 5, C is ⅓ of the way from A (distance 12, walk 4 from A → −3; midpoint −1 is a trap)

solve-q-r26-t18-01.t: A and B represent digits. Given: \overline{2A6}+\overline{B8}=\overline{3A4} B=?
solve-q-r26-t18-01.d: 2A6 + B8 = 3A4, find B (carry into the tens: same ending in a middle column → 0 or 9; plug in to check)

solve-q-r26-t18-02.t: A, B and C represent digits, and A>C>0. Which of the following could be the value of \overline{ABC}-\overline{CBA}?
solve-q-r26-t18-02.d: possible value of ABC − CBA (it equals 99(A − C): middle digit 9, outer digits sum to 9 → 495)

solve-q-r26-t18-03.t: A and B represent digits. Which of the following could be the value of \overline{A3}\times\overline{B7}?
solve-q-r26-t18-03.d: possible value of A3 × B7 (units digit 3·7 → ends in 1; size between 13·17 and 93·97 → 851)

solve-q-r26-t19-01.d: ◆(x) = x² − 2x, find ◆(x+1) (put the whole input in brackets and expand; or plug in x = 0, then x = 2)

solve-q-r26-t19-02.t: For which of the following operations is a\star b=b\star a for all numbers a and b?
solve-q-r26-t19-02.d: which operation has a⋆b = b⋆a always? (one counterexample with a = 1, b = 2 kills a choice; swap the letters to prove 'always')

solve-q-r26-t19-03.t: The operation \blacklozenge is defined for every positive integer x: \blacklozenge(x)=\begin{cases} 3x, & x \text{ odd} \\ x^2-12, & x \text{ even} \end{cases} Given: \blacklozenge(x)=24. x=?
solve-q-r26-t19-03.d: ◆(x) = 3x if odd, x² − 12 if even; ◆(x) = 24, find x (try both rules and check parity; or work back from the choices)

solve-q-r26-t19-05.d: ◆(x) = x⁵ + 3x⁴ − … − 7, find ◆(2) − ◆(−2) (full calculation; or only the odd powers survive, doubled)

solve-q-r26-t19-18.t: The operation \blacklozenge is defined for every positive number x. It is known that for every positive x: \blacklozenge(\blacklozenge(x))=x. Which of the following can be the definition of the operation \blacklozenge?
solve-q-r26-t19-18.d: ◆(◆(x)) = x, which definition fits? (put each rule on trial with x = 2; know the self-undoing families c − x and c/x)

solve-q-r26-t20-01.t: Given: x and y are positive numbers, and x>y. Which of the following must be true?
solve-q-r26-t20-01.d: x > y > 0, which must be true? (plug in 3 and 2, then ½ and ¼ from the other region; write MUST down)

solve-q-r26-t20-02.t: Given: -1<x<0. Which of the following is the smallest?
solve-q-r26-t20-02.d: −1 < x < 0, which is smallest: x³, x, −x², 1/x? (plug in x = −½; with negatives, farther from 0 is smaller)

solve-q-r26-t20-03.t: How many odd numbers are there between 20 and 80?
solve-q-r26-t20-03.d: how many odd numbers between 20 and 80? (first 21, last 79: (79 − 21)/2 + 1 = 30; or half of the 60 numbers)

solve-q-r26-t20-04.t: A drawer holds 5 red socks, 7 blue socks and 9 green socks. Dana takes socks out of the drawer without looking. What is the smallest number of socks she must take out to be sure she has two socks of the same color?
solve-q-r26-t20-04.d: 5 red, 7 blue, 9 green socks, how many to be sure of a pair? (worst luck + 1 = 4; pigeonhole)

solve-q-r26-t21-01.t: A drawer holds 10 red, 8 blue and 6 green socks. In the dark, Dana takes out socks one at a time. What is the smallest number of socks she must take out to be sure she has 3 socks of the same color?
solve-q-r26-t21-01.d: 10 red, 8 blue, 6 green socks, how many to be sure of 3 of one color? (worst luck 2+2+2, then +1 = 7; spot the traps)

solve-q-r26-t21-02.t: Five different positive integers have a sum of 20. Which of the following must be true?
solve-q-r26-t21-02.d: 5 different positive integers sum to 20, which must be true? (counterexamples from 1+2+3+4+5 = 15 plus 5 spare; prove the survivor)

solve-q-r26-t22-01.t: In a choir, the ratio of sopranos to altos is 2:3, and the ratio of altos to tenors is 4:5. There are 30 tenors. How many singers are in the choir?
solve-q-r26-t22-01.d: S:A = 2:3, A:T = 4:5, 30 tenors, total singers? (make the shared altos equal: 8:12:15 → 35x = 70)

solve-q-r26-t22-02.t: Six workers paint a hall in 10 days. All the workers work at the same rate. How many days would 4 workers need to paint the same hall?
solve-q-r26-t22-02.d: 6 workers paint a hall in 10 days, how many days for 4? (more or less first; inverse proportion: workers × days = 60 → 15)

solve-q-r26-t22-03.t: In a club, the ratio of boys to girls is 5:4. Then 10 boys leave the club, and the ratio of boys to girls becomes 5:6. How many members did the club have at first?
solve-q-r26-t22-03.d: boys:girls 5:4, 10 boys leave → 5:6, members at first? (keep the girls fixed: 15:12 and 10:12 → 54; or an equation)

solve-q-r26-t22-04.t: A pen costs x credits. A notebook costs 3 credits more than a pen. How much do y pens and y notebooks cost altogether?
solve-q-r26-t22-04.d: pen x, notebook x + 3, cost of y of each? (choose numbers x = 2, y = 3 and test choices; or build y(2x + 3))

solve-q-r26-t22-05.t: A parking lot has 30 vehicles: cars and motorcycles. Each car has 4 wheels, and each motorcycle has 2 wheels. There are 96 wheels in total. How many motorcycles are in the parking lot?
solve-q-r26-t22-05.d: 30 cars and motorcycles, 96 wheels, how many motorcycles? (assume all the same kind, then fix the difference ÷ 2)

solve-q-r26-t22-20.t: Shelf A has 26 more books than shelf B. Some books are moved from shelf A to shelf B. After the move, shelf B has 6 more books than shelf A. How many books were moved?
solve-q-r26-t22-20.d: shelf A has 26 more than B; after moving, B has 6 more, books moved? (each book changes the gap by 2: 32 ÷ 2 = 16)

solve-q-r26-t23-01.t: A price rises by 25%. Later, the new price falls by 12%. By what percent is the final price higher than the original price?
solve-q-r26-t23-01.d: price +25% then −12%, overall change? (multipliers 1.25 × 0.88 = 1.1 → 10%; or plug in 100)

solve-q-r26-t23-03.t: The price of a desk is 150% of the price of a chair. The price of a table is 150% more than the price of the chair. By what percent is the price of the table higher than the price of the desk?
solve-q-r26-t23-03.d: desk = 150% of chair, table = 150% more than chair, table vs desk? (plug in chair = 100; 'p% more' = (100+p)%)

solve-q-r26-t23-04.t: A 300-gram mixture of sugar and water is 20% sugar. How many grams of sugar must be added to make the mixture 40% sugar?
solve-q-r26-t23-04.d: 300 g mixture 20% sugar, how much sugar to reach 40%? (the water stays: 240 g = 60% → 400 g; or test the choices)

solve-q-r26-t23-05.t: A school has N students, and g of them are girls. 25% of the girls play chess. What percent of all the students are girls who play chess?
solve-q-r26-t23-05.d: N students, g girls, 25% of girls play chess, what percent of all? (plug in N = 200, g = 80; or build 25g/N)

solve-q-r26-t23-16.t: A library has only novels and textbooks, 600 books in all. 45% of the novels is the same number of books as 30% of the textbooks. How many novels does the library have?
solve-q-r26-t23-16.d: 600 books, 45% of novels = 30% of textbooks, how many novels? (flip rule: N:T = 30:45 = 2:3 → 240; check and traps)

solve-q-r26-t24-01.t: A club has 50 members. Of them, 32 swim and 27 run. At least how many members swim but do not run?
solve-q-r26-t24-01.d: 50 members, 32 swim, 27 run → at least how many swim only (make both as big as possible: 32 − 27; check on the strip)

solve-q-r26-t24-02.t: In a school, 40% of the students are in the upper grades and the rest are in the lower grades. 30% of the upper-grade students and 60% of the lower-grade students walk to school. What percent of the students who walk to school are in the upper grades?
solve-q-r26-t24-02.d: 40% upper grades, 30%/60% walk → what % of walkers are upper grade (plug in 100, two-way table; 12 of 48; traps = wrong whole)

solve-q-r26-t24-03.t: In a survey, 80% of the people own a phone, 75% own a laptop, and 70% own a tablet. At least what percent of the people own all three?
solve-q-r26-t24-03.d: 80%, 75%, 70% own phone/laptop/tablet → at least % owning all three (count who's missing: 100 − 75; or sum − 2·100)

solve-q-r26-t25-01.t: The average score of the students in a class was 70. A new student with a score of 94 joined the class, and the class average rose to 73. How many students were in the class before the new student joined?
solve-q-r26-t25-01.d: class average 70, new 94 raises it to 73 → students before (balance: 21 ÷ 3 = 7; or equation 70n + 94 = 73(n+1))

solve-q-r26-t25-02.t: Dana took five tests. Her scores on four of them were 78, 85, 91 and 88. The average of all five scores is 85. What was her score on the fifth test?
solve-q-r26-t25-02.d: scores 78, 85, 91, 88, average of five is 85 → fifth score (the balance: differences −7, 0, +6, +3; or the sum formula)

solve-q-r26-t25-03.t: Six different positive integers have an average of 9. What is the largest possible value of one of them?
solve-q-r26-t25-03.d: six different positive integers, average 9 → largest possible value (sum 54, others smallest: 1 to 5 → 39)

solve-q-r26-t25-04.t: The average of nine consecutive even numbers is 30. What is the largest of them?
solve-q-r26-t25-04.d: nine consecutive even numbers, average 30 → largest (evenly spaced: middle = 30, count up by 2 → 38)

solve-q-r26-t25-05.t: The average of a, b and c is 20. What is the average of 3a+2, 3b+2 and 3c+2?
solve-q-r26-t25-05.d: average of a, b, c is 20 → average of 3a+2, 3b+2, 3c+2 (×3 then +2 to the average; or plug in 20s)

solve-q-r26-t26-01.t: A printer finishes a job in 60 minutes. Its speed increases by 20%. How many minutes does the same job take now?
solve-q-r26-t26-01.d: printer takes 60 min, speed +20% → new time (flip the fraction: ×6/5 → time ×5/6 = 50; or pick a job size)

solve-q-r26-t26-02.t: Worker A can do a job alone in 10 hours. Worker B can do the same job alone in 15 hours. How many hours do they need if they work together?
solve-q-r26-t26-02.d: workers 10 h and 15 h together → time (sense check: between 5 and 10; times over plus: 150/25 = 6)

solve-q-r26-t26-03.t: Pipe A fills a pool in 12 hours. Pipe B fills the same pool in 6 hours. Pipe A runs alone for 3 hours, and then pipe B is also opened. How many more hours are needed to fill the pool?
solve-q-r26-t26-03.d: pipes 12 h and 6 h, A runs alone 3 h first → more hours needed (pick a job size of 12 units; or fractions)

solve-q-r26-t26-04.t: A machine makes 60 parts at a rate of 30 parts per hour, and then 60 more parts at a rate of 20 parts per hour. What is its average rate for all 120 parts, in parts per hour?
solve-q-r26-t26-04.d: 60 parts at 30/h then 60 at 20/h → average rate (total work ÷ total time = 24; estimate: weighted by time, not 25)

solve-q-r26-t26-21.t: Last month Dana spent her whole budget on notebooks and bought 30 of them. This month her budget is 20% larger, and each notebook costs 1.5 times as much as last month. How many notebooks can she buy this month with her whole budget?
solve-q-r26-t26-21.d: 30 notebooks, budget +20%, price ×1.5 → how many now (compare by factors: 30 × 6/5 × 2/3 = 24; traps explained)

solve-q-r26-t27-01.t: A train 300 meters long travels at a constant speed. It passes a signal post in 15 seconds. How many seconds does it take to cross a bridge 500 meters long completely?
solve-q-r26-t27-01.d: 300 m train passes a post in 15 s → time to cross a 500 m bridge (bridge + train = 800 m)

solve-q-r26-t27-02.t: A boat travels 48 km downstream in 2 hours. The return trip upstream, along the same route, takes 3 hours. The boat’s speed in still water does not change. What is the speed of the current, in kph?
solve-q-r26-t27-02.d: boat 48 km down in 2 h, up in 3 h → current (down = boat + current, up = boat − current; half the difference)

solve-q-r26-t27-03.t: Two cyclists start together from the same point of a circular track 1.2 km long and ride in opposite directions. Their speeds are 20 kph and 16 kph. After how many minutes do they meet for the first time?
solve-q-r26-t27-03.d: 1.2 km circular track, 20 and 16 kph opposite directions → first meeting (add speeds: 36 kph, one lap → 2 min)

solve-q-r26-t27-05.t: A cyclist rides from home to work at a constant speed. If she rode 25% faster, the trip would take 12 minutes less. How many minutes does the trip take at her usual speed?
solve-q-r26-t27-05.d: 25% faster saves 12 min → usual trip time (flip the fraction: speed ×5/4 → time ×4/5, 20% = 12 → 60; check with numbers)

solve-q-r26-t27-06.t: A car travels d kilometers in t hours. At the same speed, how many minutes does it take to travel k kilometers?
solve-q-r26-t27-06.d: d km in t hours → minutes for k km, letter answers (plug in d = 40, t = 2, k = 10; or algebra)

solve-q-r26-t27-31.t: A delivery van travels 3 times as far as a scooter, at 1.5 times the scooter's speed. The scooter's trip takes 40 minutes. How many minutes does the van's trip take?
solve-q-r26-t27-31.d: van goes 3× as far at 1.5× the speed, scooter 40 min → van's time (the V in a speed table; or compare by factors → 80)

solve-q-r26-t28-04.t: A code has 4 digits. Each digit is from 0 to 9, digits may repeat, and the code may start with 0. How many codes contain the digit 5 at least once?
solve-q-r26-t28-04.d: 4-digit codes 0–9 with the digit 5 at least once (all minus none: 10⁴ − 9⁴ = 3439)

solve-q-r26-t28-05.t: Five different letters are put into 3 mailboxes. A mailbox may get any number of letters, or none. In how many different ways can the letters be put into the mailboxes?
solve-q-r26-t28-05.d: 5 different letters into 3 mailboxes (each letter chooses a box: 3⁵; check a small case)

solve-q-r26-t28-06.t: Six different books are placed on a shelf in a row. The 3 math books among them must stand together, in any order. How many arrangements are possible?
solve-q-r26-t28-06.d: 6 books in a row, 3 math books together (glue into a block: 4! × 3! = 144)

solve-q-r26-t28-07.t: Three boys and two girls stand in a row. All five are different people. The two girls may not stand next to each other. How many orders are possible?
solve-q-r26-t28-07.d: 3 boys, 2 girls in a row, girls not side by side (gaps between the boys; or all minus together: 120 − 48)

solve-q-r26-t28-08.t: How many different arrangements of all the letters of the word BANANA are there? (An arrangement does not have to be a real word.)
solve-q-r26-t28-08.d: arrangements of BANANA (6! divided by each repeat's factorial: 720 ÷ (3!·2!) = 60)

solve-q-r26-t28-09.t: Six people sit around a round table. Two arrangements are the same if one is a rotation of the other. Dana and Eli must sit next to each other. How many arrangements are possible?
solve-q-r26-t28-09.d: 6 people at a round table, Dana and Eli together (glue, then (n−1)!: 4!·2 = 48; or fix Dana)

solve-q-r26-t28-28.d: (10! − 9!)/8! (take out the smaller factorial: 9!·(10 − 1); or write all in 8!s: 90 − 9 = 81)

solve-q-r26-t29-01.t: In a class of 30 students, 12 play soccer, 10 play chess, and 4 play both. One student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student plays soccer or chess?
solve-q-r26-t29-01.d: 30 students, 12 soccer, 10 chess, 4 both → P(soccer or chess) (add, subtract the overlap; or two circles)

solve-q-r26-t29-02.t: Dan answers 3 multiple-choice questions by guessing. Each question has 4 choices, and exactly one of them is correct. What is the probability that Dan answers at least one question correctly?
solve-q-r26-t29-02.d: guessing 3 questions with 4 choices, P(at least one correct) (1 minus none: 1 − 27/64)

solve-q-r26-t29-03.t: Box A contains 2 red balls and 3 white balls. Box B contains 3 red balls and 1 white ball. A fair coin is tossed: on heads, a ball is drawn at random from box A; on tails, a ball is drawn at random from box B. What is the probability that the ball is red?
solve-q-r26-t29-03.d: coin picks box A (2R,3W) or box B (3R,1W), P(red) (tree: multiply along branches, add; don't pour boxes together)

solve-q-r26-t30-01.t: In the accompanying figure, lines a and b are both perpendicular to line c. Line d crosses lines a and b. What is the value of x?
solve-q-r26-t30-01.d: a ⊥ c and b ⊥ c, transversal with 50°, find x (prove a ∥ b, then small + large = 180° → 130°)

solve-q-r26-t30-02.t: Points A, B, C and D lie on a line in this order, as shown in the accompanying figure. Given: \begin{cases} AC=11 \\ BD=14 \\ AD=20 \end{cases} What is the length of BC?
solve-q-r26-t30-02.d: 4 points on a line, AC = 11, BD = 14, AD = 20 → BC (step by step; or AC + BD = AD + BC)

solve-q-r26-t30-03.t: In the accompanying figure, a\parallel b. What is the value of x?
solve-q-r26-t30-03.d: zig-zag with two bends between parallel lines, find x (left angles = right angles: 40 + 65 = x + 35; or parallel lines through bends)

solve-q-r26-t31-01.t: Triangle ABC is right at C, and CD is the altitude to AB. Given: \begin{cases} AC=15\text{ cm} \\ BC=20\text{ cm} \\ AB=25\text{ cm} \end{cases} What is CD (in cm)?
solve-q-r26-t31-01.d: right triangle 15-20-25, altitude CD to hypotenuse (area two ways: leg × leg = hypotenuse × altitude → 12)

solve-q-r26-t31-02.t: In triangle ABC: \begin{cases} AB=6\text{ cm} \\ BC=8\text{ cm} \end{cases} Which of the following could be the area of the triangle (in cm²)?
solve-q-r26-t31-02.d: sides 6 and 8, no angle: which could be the area? (height ≤ 6, so area ≤ 24 → 20)

solve-q-r26-t31-03.t: In triangle ABC: \begin{cases} AB=6\text{ cm} \\ BC=7\text{ cm} \\ AC=10\text{ cm} \end{cases} Which of the following is true?
solve-q-r26-t31-03.d: sides 6, 7, 10: acute, right or obtuse? (compare 10² with 6² + 7²; obtuse angle is opposite the longest side)

solve-q-r26-t32-01.d: parallelogram, sides 10 and 14, angle 150°, area (extend the base, 30° next to it → height = half of 10 → 70)

solve-q-r26-t32-02.t: A right trapezoid: one height, one triple
solve-q-r26-t32-02.d: right trapezoid, bases 9 and 15, leg 10, area (drop a height: 6-8-10 triple → height 8 → 96)

solve-q-r26-t32-06.t: A staircase has the perimeter of its rectangle
solve-q-r26-t32-06.d: staircase figure 12 wide, 8 tall, all right angles → perimeter (push the steps out: 2(12 + 8) = 40)
